detail:
Mayo Clinic describes two broad categories of migraine medicine. Acute (pain-relieving) treatments are taken during an attack and work best early; they include pain relievers, triptans, and oral CGRP antagonists such as ubrogepant and rimegepant. Preventive medicines are taken regularly to reduce how often attacks happen, how severe they are, and how long they last, and are usually considered when attacks are frequent, long-lasting, or not responding to acute treatment.

Preventive options Mayo lists include blood-pressure medicines such as beta blockers, anti-seizure medicines such as topiramate, certain antidepressants, CGRP monoclonal antibodies given monthly or every three months, and, specifically for chronic migraine, onabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) injections about every 12 weeks. Mayo also notes some migraine medicines are not safe in pregnancy, one of several reasons selection is a clinician's decision.

Talk to your doctor before starting or changing any medication.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material.
summary: Mayo Clinic divides migraine treatment into acute medicines taken during an attack and preventive treatment taken regularly; for chronic migraine, preventive options include CGRP-targeting medicines and onabotulinumtoxinA injections about every 12 weeks.
takeaways: acute medicines work best taken early in an attack
preventives aim to cut how often and how hard attacks hit
cgrp medicines are a newer preventive class your doctor may discuss
never start, switch, or stop migraine medicines without your doctor
title: Migraine management: acute plus preventive treatment
